clinicalPearls: Pulmonary capillaritis is the commonest histological pattern underlying immune-mediated diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, defined by neutrophilic infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the alveolar septal capillaries.

The classic triad is haemoptysis, falling haemoglobin and diffuse alveolar (ground-glass) infiltrates, but haemoptysis is absent in a substantial minority, so it should not be relied on to exclude the diagnosis.
Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage returning progressively bloodier aliquots confirms alveolar haemorrhage even when the patient is not coughing blood.
Haemosiderin-laden macrophages on lavage indicate that bleeding has been present for some duration rather than being purely acute.

There is a strong association with ANCA-associated vasculitis (especially microscopic polyangiitis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis) and with anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, so ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and complement should be checked urgently.
Gas transfer (DLCO/KCO) is characteristically elevated during active haemorrhage because intra-alveolar blood avidly takes up inhaled carbon monoxide.
It must be separated from bland alveolar haemorrhage (no capillaritis, e.g. mitral valve disease or coagulopathy) and from diffuse alveolar damage, as management differs.
Always screen for coexisting glomerulonephritis, because a pulmonary-renal syndrome dramatically changes urgency and treatment.
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary capillaritis is a small-vessel vasculitis of the alveolar septa in which neutrophils infiltrate the interstitium and undergo leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust), accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis of the capillary walls and fibrin thrombi. Disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane allows red cells and fibrin to flood the alveolar spaces, producing diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. It is most often immune-mediated: ANCA-associated vasculitides (microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, frequently with myeloperoxidase or proteinase-3 antibodies), anti-glomerular basement membrane (Goodpasture) disease, systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases, IgA vasculitis, the antiphospholipid syndrome, and drug-induced forms (for example propylthiouracil and hydralazine). A pauci-immune isolated (idiopathic) variant occurs without systemic disease. Neutrophil activation, complement engagement and endothelial injury drive the capillary destruction, and repeated episodes can lead to interstitial fibrosis and haemosiderosis.
additionalDifferentials: Bland diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (mitral stenosis, coagulopathy or anticoagulation) without capillaritis
Diffuse alveolar damage with haemorrhage (acute respiratory distress syndrome)
Haemorrhagic infective pneumonia (e.g. invasive aspergillosis, leptospirosis, severe influenza)
Intrathoracic malignancy causing haemorrhage (e.g. angiosarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma)
additionalInvestigations: Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage showing increasingly haemorrhagic returns and haemosiderin-laden macrophages
Autoimmune serology: ANCA (myeloperoxidase and proteinase-3), anti-GBM antibody, ANA and dsDNA, complement, antiphospholipid antibodies
Urinalysis with microscopy and renal function to detect an accompanying glomerulonephritis
High-resolution CT of the chest (bilateral ground-glass opacification and consolidation)
Full blood count for falling haemoglobin and a coagulation screen
Gas transfer measurement, which is typically raised in acute alveolar haemorrhage
Surgical (video-assisted thoracoscopic) lung biopsy when the diagnosis is unclear, to confirm capillaritis versus bland haemorrhage
redFlags: Rapidly falling haemoglobin with worsening hypoxaemia, signalling catastrophic alveolar haemorrhage
Concurrent acute kidney injury or an active urinary sediment, indicating a pulmonary-renal syndrome
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause and on how quickly immunosuppression is started; isolated pauci-immune capillaritis and treated ANCA-associated disease often respond well, but recurrent haemorrhage or progression to respiratory failure or end-stage renal disease carries appreciable mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming that the absence of haemoptysis excludes alveolar haemorrhage, when infiltrates plus anaemia should already raise suspicion.
Attributing bilateral infiltrates to infection or fluid overload and thereby delaying serology and immunosuppression.
Relying on a small transbronchial biopsy, which is usually inadequate to confirm or exclude capillaritis.
Failing to screen the kidneys and missing a treatable pulmonary-renal syndrome.
Overlooking a drug trigger such as propylthiouracil or hydralazine.
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
ATS/ERS statements on diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and the pulmonary vasculitides
management: Urgent pulsed corticosteroids to control immune-mediated diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Induction immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for ANCA-associated and other severe capillaritis
Plasma exchange for anti-glomerular basement membrane disease and for severe or refractory alveolar haemorrhage with renal involvement
Supportive care for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with oxygen, transfusion, correction of coagulopathy and mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure
Identify the underlying cause with targeted serology including ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complement and antiphospholipid antibodies, and treat accordingly
Concurrent management of associated glomerulonephritis with nephrology input and renal replacement where needed

Maintenance immunosuppression with monitoring for relapse and treatment-related infection, including opportunistic infection prophylaxis, within a multidisciplinary respiratory, rheumatology and nephrology team
